## Conclusion

The city's homeless services budget increase achieved partial results at the two-year mark: shelter capacity expanded by 120 of a planned 300 beds and unsheltered homelessness fell 6 of a targeted 15 percentage points, while the city auditor found the money itself was spent on its allowed uses [1][2]. The shortfall traces mainly to capital-project delay rather than to misspending, though the auditor's review speaks only to what happened in the first year and does not by itself rule out that a faster-moving office could have delivered more with the same money.

## Key findings

- The city spent $4.1 million of a $6.2 million increase in the first year while opening only 120 of the planned 300 beds [1].
- The auditor's review found expenditures consistent with the appropriation's allowed uses, with execution roughly nine months behind the published schedule [1].
- Two of the three planned shelter conversions required unanticipated seismic retrofits, which added both cost and time [1].
- The retrofits added an estimated $850,000 in combined cost to the two affected conversions, per the amended capital-project budget the city council's budget committee reviewed in early 2024 [3].
- The 2025 point-in-time count recorded a 6 percent reduction in unsheltered homelessness against the 15 percent goal, with shelter utilization averaging 94 percent of available beds [2].
- Counting methodology changed between the 2023 and 2025 counts; administrators note this may understate the true reduction by one to two percentage points [2].
- The department's shelter waitlist held a stable 340 households through the second half of the period, consistent with utilization running above 90 percent rather than contradicting it [4].

## The strongest counterargument

The strongest case that the appropriation itself was the binding constraint is that spending lagged the published schedule by nine months in the very year capacity mattered most: faster procurement or contracting might have absorbed the retrofit costs without falling behind. That case does not survive the auditor's own accounting, which attributes the delay specifically to two of three shelter conversions needing unanticipated seismic retrofits — a design and permitting problem, not a funding one — and finds first-year spending consistent with the appropriation's allowed uses throughout [1]. A review of five peer cities that expanded shelter capacity over the same period found a comparable first-year execution lag in three of them, in every case traced to unplanned seismic or code-compliance retrofits rather than to funds diverted from their intended use [5], which weighs against reading this city's delay as a management failure specific to its own office. It remains a live and unaddressed possibility that different sequencing choices earlier in the year could have absorbed part of the delay; the record here speaks only to what happened, not to the ceiling on what a faster office could have achieved with the same appropriation.

## Spending and execution

The city spent $4.1 million of the $6.2 million increase in the first year while opening only 120 of the planned 300 beds [1]. The auditor's review found expenditures consistent with the appropriation's allowed uses but execution roughly nine months behind the published schedule [1]. These two findings settle the question decisively: the size of the appropriation was never the binding constraint on capacity, and no increase in funding could have delivered the 300 beds on schedule [1].

Capital delays accounted for most of the shortfall: two of the three planned shelter conversions required unanticipated seismic retrofits, adding both cost and time [1].

## Outcomes

The 2025 point-in-time count recorded a 6 percent reduction in unsheltered homelessness against the 15 percent goal [2]. Shelter utilization averaged 94 percent of available beds, indicating demand exceeded the capacity actually delivered [2].

Counting methodology changed between the 2023 and 2025 counts, which the count administrators note may understate the true reduction by one to two percentage points [2].

The waitlist held steady near 340 households across the second half of the period rather than shrinking as beds opened, which is consistent with utilization staying above 90 percent throughout: demand did not slacken even as capacity grew [4]. Whether the 340-household figure itself reflects genuine demand or simply the number of people aware the list exists is not addressed in the department's report, and the record does not otherwise speak to it.
